entries.finding: A 2026 dose-response systematic review and meta-analysis included 15 randomized studies with 962 participants diagnosed with depression and evaluated vitamin D supplementation against placebo for depressive symptoms.
Across the 15 studies, vitamin D supplementation improved depressive symptom scores versus placebo with a pooled SMD of -0.98 (95% CI -1.28 to -0.68; p<0.001).

The pooled vitamin D depression effect had high between-study heterogeneity (I²=79%; p<0.001), so the estimate should not be treated as a uniform effect across populations, regimens, or baseline vitamin D status.
Secondary pooled outcomes showed reductions in serum PTH (MD -4.19 pg/mL; 95% CI -8.18 to -0.20) and TNF-α (MD -0.30 pg/mL; 95% CI -0.44 to -0.16) with vitamin D supplementation.

The dose-response analysis associated higher daily vitamin D doses up to about 5,000 IU/day with greater depressive-symptom reduction within the studied trials, while BMI, body weight, and IL-6 did not show significant pooled changes; this does not establish a universally optimal dose.

A systematic review and meta-analysis included five randomized controlled trials with 474 participants; three trials involved depression with significant medical comorbidity and two involved primary depressive disorders.
Coenzyme Q10 supplementation reduced depressive symptoms versus control with a pooled SMD of -0.68 (95% CI -1.02 to -0.33; p<0.01; I²=58%).

Sensitivity analysis indicated that much of the heterogeneity in the CoQ10 depression meta-analysis was driven by a single study, limiting confidence in a uniform effect across the diverse included clinical populations.
Coenzyme Q10 did not show a statistically significant pooled benefit for fatigue (SMD -0.33; 95% CI -1.38 to 0.72; p=0.54; I²=89%), and this outcome was based on only two trials.
A 2025 systematic review identified 19 randomized-trial articles involving 897 participants, with 18 studies contributing to meta-analysis of L-theanine and sleep outcomes.
L-theanine produced a small statistically significant improvement in subjective sleep-onset latency (SMD 0.15; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.29; p=0.04; 10 studies).
L-theanine improved subjective daytime dysfunction in the sleep meta-analysis (SMD 0.33; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.49; p<0.001; 9 studies).
Overall subjective sleep-quality scores improved with L-theanine (SMD 0.43; 95% CI 0.04 to 0.83; p=0.03; 12 studies).

The authors noted a lack of studies using pure L-theanine and insufficient evidence to determine an adequate dose and duration, so sleep findings should not be generalized across mixed formulations or treated as an established dosing recommendation.
A 2025 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis included 41 randomized controlled trial articles with 2,049 adult participants evaluating psyllium and lipid outcomes.
Psyllium reduced total cholesterol by a pooled weighted mean difference of -9.05 (95% CI -13.71 to -4.40; p<0.05) in the included adult trials.
Psyllium reduced LDL cholesterol by a pooled weighted mean difference of -8.55 (95% CI -12.92 to -4.19; p<0.001).
Pooled changes in HDL cholesterol (WMD 0.57; 95% CI -0.88 to 2.04) and triglycerides (WMD -5.29; 95% CI -12.14 to 1.54) were not statistically significant.

Heterogeneity was considerable for total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, and triglyceride estimates (I² roughly 78% to 89%), and dose and duration did not show a significant linear relationship with lipid outcomes.
In randomized placebo-controlled trials of purified berberine for metabolic-syndrome components, triglycerides decreased by a pooled WMD of -0.367 mmol/L (95% CI -0.560 to -0.175; p<0.001).
Berberine reduced fasting plasma glucose by a pooled WMD of -0.515 mmol/L (95% CI -0.847 to -0.183; p=0.002) in the metabolic-syndrome meta-analysis.
Berberine reduced waist circumference by a pooled WMD of -3.270 cm (95% CI -4.818 to -1.722; p<0.001).
Secondary lipid outcomes favored berberine for LDL cholesterol (WMD -0.495 mmol/L; 95% CI -0.714 to -0.276) and total cholesterol (WMD -0.451 mmol/L; 95% CI -0.631 to -0.271), both p<0.001.

The same placebo-controlled meta-analysis found no statistically significant pooled effect of berberine on HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, or diastolic blood pressure, limiting broad cardiometabolic claims.

No significant difference in safety outcomes was observed between berberine and placebo; subgroup/meta-regression signals suggested short-term treatment (≤90 days) differed for some lipid outcomes, and more high-quality randomized trials were recommended.
